job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Kira Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the office in Guadalajara by nine. Tiendaya is an online shop platform with sixty people, and I'm a junior developer on the checkout team. I write small features and fix bugs, with an AI assistant doing the first draft of most of my code, and my lead Mauricio reviews it. I finished software engineering last summer with a plain pass and no internship, but I won a university hackathon, which is how I got hired. I share a flat with my cousin Paola, and on Sundays it's mass and lunch at my grandmother's, with twenty relatives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we find out who actually builds things. Less noise, more real work. At work I'd say fine, we keep going. Online I'd post that hype is cheap and businesses are hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be fine. I'd keep my developer job, and keep using AI as the good tool it is. If AI is only a good tool, I keep my job and my worries stay the same ordinary ones, like rent and my loan. The loan is 180,000 pesos, and I send my mum 2,000 each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Tiendaya, save 3,000 pesos a month, and work on my side idea, a booking app for small salons like my aunt's. I'd launch it in two years. I'd keep helping my mum and keep going to my grandmother's on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. A bit restless, because I'm impatient to grow. Mostly happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a booking app for salons?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt Lupita runs a salon with six chairs and keeps appointments in a paper diary and on WhatsApp. She loses about ten bookings a week to mix-ups. I could build her something in a month, and then sell it to the other salons on her street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you fund it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nights and weekends, no outside money. If it takes off, I'd go part time at Tiendaya, and then leave. My family would say stay in a safe job, and my grandmother would pray for me. But I like building my own thing, and I believe in working hard for your own.

say: I'd say good: now we find out who actually **builds things**.
Online I'd post that hype is cheap and businesses are hard.
think: If AI is only a good tool, my job stays and my worries are **ordinary**: rent and the loan.
The loan is **180,000 pesos**, and I send my mum 2,000 each month.
do: Keep working at Tiendaya and save **3,000 pesos** a month.
Build a **booking app** for small salons like my aunt's and launch in two years.
Keep helping my mum and going to Sunday lunch.
feel: Good, a bit **restless**, impatient to grow.
S0.quote: If AI is only a good tool, I keep my job and my worries stay the same ordinary ones, like rent and my loan.
fieldNote: Plateau suits her; the **side business** is already her plan.
Family help exists and she half-uses it: she sends **money** to her mum.
Entrepreneurial streak shows from the first answer.

steps.text: Keep working on the checkout team at Tiendaya
Save 3,000 pesos a month
Build a booking app for my aunt Lupita's salon
Keep sending my mum 2,000 pesos a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say bring it on, but be fair. Firms should let people use AI openly and not punish them for it. At work I'd say let's build with it. Online I'd say learn it or be left behind, which people might find harsh, but it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the junior part of my job, writing small features, is what AI does best now. My lead could ask one senior to do what three of us do. I'm a plain-pass junior, and the hackathon helped me get in, but it won't keep me in. I'd have to move up fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on bigger tasks, learn how to design systems, and use the AI to do three things at once, which makes me look more productive. I'd push the salon app too, because I'd rather own something than be replaced. I'd save 3,500 pesos a month and learn to sell, since a developer who can sell is rare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but fired up. It feels like the start of a race.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does moving up fast look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Asking my lead for the hardest bug on the board every week, and fixing it with the AI and my head. If I can solve what the AI gets wrong, my lead will keep me. I'd also tell him my aim is to lead a team in three years, so he knows I'm not just coasting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if it doesn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the next company, or my own. I'm not afraid of changing jobs. My mum says a company owes you a salary and you owe it good work, nothing else.

say: I'd say bring it on, but firms should let people use AI **openly**.
Online I'd say learn it or be left behind, which is harsh but true.
think: Writing small features is what AI does best, so one **senior** could do the work of three juniors.
The hackathon helped me get in, but it won't keep me in.
do: Take on **bigger tasks** and learn system design.
Push the **salon app** so I own something.
Save 3,500 pesos a month and learn to sell.
feel: Uneasy but fired up, like the start of a **race**.
S1.quote: If I can solve what the AI gets wrong, my lead will keep me.
fieldNote: Her answer is **ownership**: move up, or build her own thing.
Not loyal to a company by principle, only to good work.
Says it bluntly online, though she knows it sounds harsh.

steps.text: Ask Mauricio for the hardest open bug every week
Push the salon booking app to its first five paying salons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest opportunity and the biggest risk we've seen. The government shouldn't hold back founders, it should help new businesses start, not pay people to sit at home. At work I'd say let's use it to build things before somebody else does. At church I'd pray, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job as a junior developer is gone in two years, or turned into AI supervisor. A plain-pass degree, no internship, and a loan. I'd compete with software that never sleeps, so I'd have to move before my layoff, not after it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the salon business full time, or as full as I could. I'd save 5,000 pesos a month, cut outings, and ask my family to help in a pinch. I'd approach fifty salons in the first three months, and keep my job as long as I could to pay the loan. Hands-on businesses like salons last until about 2031, so my customers would be safe longer than I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly, but wired. I'd wake at four, and instead of lying there I'd get up and work on the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't that a risky bet with a loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and my family would say so. But sitting still is the bigger risk. If my job's going away anyway, I'd rather spend my last paid months building something that's mine than polishing my CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd tell me to be careful and light a candle. Then she'd ask how much I need, and offer her savings, which I'd refuse and then accept. Our family is like that: loud about worry and quiet about help.

say: I'd say it's the biggest opportunity and the biggest risk, and government should help **new businesses** start.
think: My junior developer job is gone in **two years**, or becomes AI supervising.
I'd have to move **before** my layoff, not after it.
do: Start the salon business full time and approach **fifty salons** in three months.
Save **5,000 pesos** a month and cut outings.

feel: Alarmed but **wired**: I'd get up at four and work on the app.
S2.quote: If my job's going away anyway, I'd rather spend my last paid months building something that's mine than polishing my CV.
fieldNote: Fear becomes **action**: she builds rather than waits.

Family help is offered quietly and she half-accepts it.

steps.text: Pitch the booking app to fifty salons in three months
Save 5,000 pesos a month while still employed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is just right. I'd say governments should get out of the way of builders and help people retrain. At work I'd say we should take on AI projects now, while we have a head start. Online I'd post how to learn to code with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 27 and in a good place. I'd have five years of building, probably my own small company, and a name. The entry-level jobs will be gone, but I'd be on the other side of it. I'd feel lucky and a bit guilty about the people who weren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work at Tiendaya two more years to learn, and build the salon app at nights. I'd save 4,000 pesos a month and put it in an index fund. Then I'd go full time on my own company in year three. I'd also hope to marry around 2030, because my family expects it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, and fired up. It feels like my moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you feel guilty about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people like my cousin Paola, who is a cashier, wouldn't have the same chance. I'd want to help her learn, and I'd hire from my own family and street, because I don't want to build something that only works for people like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm too sure of myself. I haven't run a company, and five years of confidence can turn into five years of mistakes. I'd find a mentor, someone older who has failed once, because I trust people who've failed.

At work I'd say take on AI projects now, while we have a **head start**.

Entry-level jobs will be gone, but I'd be on the other side of it.

Go full time on my own company in year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty of time to build something. I'd say people shouldn't wait for the government, they should start learning now. At work I'd say let's play the long game. At church I'd say thank you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be great, honestly. By 2036 I'd be 32, running a company with people I know, maybe with a child. AI will be everywhere, and I'd have grown up with it. My concern is for people who don't learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and growing the app, save 3,000 pesos a month, buy a small flat and marry. I'd also help my mum retire and pay for my cousins to learn to code. I'd vote for whoever cut red tape for small firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. It's the picture I'd choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing you'd most want to be different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people in my family trust me enough to try things. My uncle thinks anything new is a scam. I'd want a world where it's okay to be curious, and where those who aren't aren't punished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To work hard and to build, not just to consume. I'd teach my children how to use the tools, but also how to think without them, like writing a letter by hand. And to call their grandmother on Sundays.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Even with a plan, two years isn't enough to build a business, pay off my loan and help my mum. What would help is room for people to start small firms, easier loans for first-time founders, and family and church that help in a pinch. I'd also want the big firms to keep hiring juniors a while longer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people shouldn't wait to be rescued. Whatever happens, the ones who start building something, a skill, a business, a small side income, will be in a better place. I'd say start small, start now, and call your family.

headlineQuote: Whatever happens, the ones who start building something, a skill, a business, a small side income, will be in a better place.
portrait: **Kira**, 22, is a junior developer in Guadalajara with a plain degree, a hackathon win and a **loan**.
Traditional and market-minded, she believes in hard work, ownership and **family**, and uses AI every day.
She meets every scenario by trying to build her own thing, starting with a **booking app** for salons like her aunt's.
Her mood is calm when she has time, but **alarmed** at two years, when her junior job would be first to go.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, where there is not enough time to build a business, repay her loan and help her mum.
whatWouldHelp: Room and easier **loans** for first-time founders, and family help in a pinch.
Big firms that keep hiring **juniors** a while longer.
